author: monster
text_post: Robert Williams is awesome my favorite of his: Quote:A full description of the painting would be in order. This tableau-vivant takes place in a circus tent, obviously the quarters of our red clown. The back drop and floor are made up of olive-tan canvas. This material serves two functions. First, it gives the observer the impression that everything about the environment is transient, ready to be moved to the next location. And secondly, the surrounding canvas has a green tint which emphasizes the image of the clown’s red costume. It might be pointed out that this carmine red figure of derision and the similarity to the devil is no coincidence. In the tent, as incidentals, is a trunk, along with papier mâché masks and grotesque, illogical theatrical props. The furniture is sparse and the floor is littered with wine bottles. The clown stands posed with a bird cage in hand. This raises the question, “Where is the bird?” He boldly smiles at the visiting show girl, as he alarms her with the cage’s contents. It is occupied with a harmless yellow corn snake. This is the visual structure of the oil painting. This melodramatic scene was paraphrased with these remarks: “Occupying the cerebral netherworld between humor and severity, the scarlet clad anti-Puck, clowns around as sole purveyor of an abstract levity with ambiguous jokes that seem audienceless.” This last quotation sheds light on the clown’s bizarre psychology. If you haven’t noticed, the clown has only one leg. He has apparently adjusted to this infirmity and incorporated it into his act. His thin left leg, wearing a red shoe, is actually his crutch. Lying on his steamer trunk is his formal prosthesis used for everyday life. The floor is strewn with booze bottles—he is apparently an unrepentant alcoholic—but that would be a simple situation if his psychosis ended there. It is obvious that he is an experienced master comedian. His costume is the classical European Scaramouche style with a half-mask nose. And of course, he wears the mask drawn back on his forehead with the long nose protruding like a horn, knowingly making himself look ominous. Two things are unmistakable. To begin with, he delights in the girl’s shock, with her surprise in the bird cage. And, his condition—he’s drunk. It is evident that this character has a second life; however, what is not so conspicuous is that this performer probably functions secretly as another clown, a more inculpable form of buffoon. The girl’s presence in his tent is not only stimulating to him, but is not an accident. Her lure to his web was, no doubt, consensual. This clown, when not entertaining a layman public, has conditioned himself, over the period of a long career, to mentally slip into a sardonic demi-humor—this is a joke realm more suited to extreme irony with a lack of moral logic. Here is a statement from the painting’s prologue verifying this: “Those private moments shared when a rubber chicken is given a Fleet enema.” Even detractors to this artwork realize that his image seems to have meaning beyond this graphic melodrama. Looking at the birdcage, the question remains, “Where is the bird?” The show girl instantly knew—it’s in the snake."

author: Slick Shimmer
text_post: There are some pretty great groups on facebook devoted to murals and street art.  These forms of art will always be the most political and subversive. As I recall, South American countries seem to have some of the most incredible images.  What you should do is search art galleries and mural/graffiti/street artists and then check out the groups those people subscribe to.  Keep looking around, it is exactly what I did.  I haven't used Facebook for several years so I don't remember any of the names.  As far as decorating, I can't recommend anything for you personally, everyone's tastes are different. I would like to mention Yoji Shinkawa however. He is responsible for the artistic direction of the Metal Gear videogame saga. For those unaware, the series focuses on Nuclear proliferation and the advancement of military technology.  The series runs the gamut of sociopolitical concepts, the nature of killing, and the realities of war economies. The characters in the series are dogs of war: damaged mercenaries, child soldiers, spies and killers.  While the art doesn't necessarily depict political concepts, Yoji's art expresses a certain masculine stoicism.  It's heavily stylized, relying chiefly on ink and whiteout to produce vibrant and memorable imagery.  He's been drawing the characters for the series since 1998. There are tons of memorable and iconic images.  You can find full scans of his artbooks if you look around. Here's a look at his process...

author: Lizard King
text_post: It is down to personal taste, we should decorate our homes to please ourselves. I'll tell you what I do. I have collected many 'clip frames' of various sizes, postcard to A5A6. Using a reasonable printer and glossy printer paper I print images that I like. Ranging from copies of famous art, characters from films I like, people of cultural significance old and new, etc.  What they all have in common is that they please my eye, and/or have some significance to me and my tastes/desires etc. There really is no limit.  They often become conversation starters for guests and potential lays. I have a few of attractive women I like which often get girls talking. Eg: "Who is that girl?". One girl once even asked if a postcard size photo of Mickey and Mallory from the movie Natural Born Killers was a photo of me and an old girlfriend.  Most of the clip frames I have were picked up for next to nothing from charity(thrift) shops. I have spent less than £50 in this endeavour. The only difficulty was playing around with the image settings before printing in order to get good results. This approach might not be for you, but I have found it very effective.
